If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175780 :question/problem "Find an eigenvector of 
![](images/cc/cc6a84d8a040240089d946999190e4d118fee2be70df2958a6a59d6534bcf429.svg)
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-3+4\textrm{i}.$" :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-3+4\textrm{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ -4 & -3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-3+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -3+4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4\text{i} & 4 \\ -4 & -4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4\text{i}{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}-4\text{i}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-3+4\textrm{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another.

As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
x_1 = -\textrm{i}x_2.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

![](images/1c/1c7fa984e0d00619ea2e8647f560efc3f928b643875f0cbf973ca8bb2a931e3e.svg)

Setting $x_2=1,$ we get the eigenvector ![](images/ec/ec3f75c25f412d466b7acfc4810ecf6987038a23ee5da0dfdd98cc181e37e0c7.svg)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175782 :question/problem "Let ![](images/53/5337ed67f212c0029ae2317c658672aa3f3f68a7614c8ce4dfafb6e92d2f2229.svg) and ![](images/4f/4fad8749e9d06a4cafdd089e6ed982131a8957fff201d865fb9da323c5c27bf5.svg) be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
![](images/a0/a05c08cb757f62c9b874fce3b3ae9db1d4278f1f96194a3e92df0a4d457b591c.svg)
Given that $\lambda_1=4+5\textrm{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of ${\dfrac{a_1a_2}{b_1b_2}}.$" :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda_1 =4+5\textrm{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ -5 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4+5\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 4+5\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5\text{i} & 5 \\ -5 & -5\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-5\text{i}{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}-5\text{i}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(4+5\textrm{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another.

As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
x_2 = \textrm{i}x_1.
$$

So, the general solution is given by

![](images/33/334bab555d470ebcc0d36eb4e2140530d4f92b2fa13e4adbfea848250d92de7b.svg)

Setting $x_1=1,$ we get the eigenvector

![](images/82/82d57d12bd8027fc3c7e9b368b752616ed33ffcce577b956c91cb8a721dd5905.svg) 

Now, since $\lambda_1=4+5\textrm{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the complex conjugate of $\lambda_1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\lambda_2=\overline{\lambda_1}=4-5\textrm{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector must be the complex conjugate of $\mathbf v_1.$ Therefore, we have

![](images/8c/8cd66a9324ee5cf95277457fc1eef8ddb30d36543b71d4446eb93b5a2d8313a7.svg)

Finally, we obtain

$$
{\dfrac{a_1a_2}{b_1b_2}} = {\dfrac{(1)(1)}{(\textrm{i})(-\textrm{i})}} = 1.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176575 :question/problem "Determine whether $v=[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}].$
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?" :question/worked-solution "The eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2+2\text{i} \\ 4-4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2{\text{i}}^{2}+2\text{i} \\ 4-4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i}(2-2\text{i}) \\ 2(2-2\text{i})\end{aligned}] \\  & =(2-2\text{i})[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =(2-2\text{i})v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=(2-2\text{i})v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =2-2\text{i}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175588 :answer-field/correct "answer-58a69195-600a-5e46-b79b-827cb7f39b55" :answer-field/choices ["answer-05a52154-a704-5e15-a11d-70a80d71913b" "answer-4f8367f4-f25a-5797-be99-f2deef2ca2c1" "answer-395b71eb-934f-50c8-901b-d659116b2b06" "answer-58a69195-600a-5e46-b79b-827cb7f39b55"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-05a52154-a704-5e15-a11d-70a80d71913b" :answer/id #uuid "05a52154-a704-5e15-a11d-70a80d71913b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\lambda =1+\text{i}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4f8367f4-f25a-5797-be99-f2deef2ca2c1" :answer/id #uuid "4f8367f4-f25a-5797-be99-f2deef2ca2c1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\lambda =1-\text{i}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-395b71eb-934f-50c8-901b-d659116b2b06" :answer/id #uuid "395b71eb-934f-50c8-901b-d659116b2b06" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\lambda =2+2\text{i}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-58a69195-600a-5e46-b79b-827cb7f39b55" :answer/id #uuid "58a69195-600a-5e46-b79b-827cb7f39b55" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\lambda =2-2\text{i}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176481 :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-2\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 4 \\ -26 & -10\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10+2\text{i} & 4 \\ -26 & -10+2\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(10+2\text{i}){x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ -26{x}_{1}+(-10+2\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A+2\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}(5+\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -\frac{1}{2}(5+\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{5+\text{i}}{-2}=-\frac{5}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\text{i}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186351201 :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-1+3\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 \\ 13 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-1+3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -1+3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2-3\text{i} & -1 \\ 13 & 2-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(-2-3\text{i}){x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0 \\ 13{x}_{1}+(2-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-1+3\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-2-3\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -(2+3\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2+3\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{-1}{2+3\text{i}}=\frac{-(2-3\text{i})}{13}=-\frac{2}{13}+\frac{3}{13}\text{i}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186326746 :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=1-3\text{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ -15 & -5\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1-3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1-3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6+3\text{i} & 3 \\ -15 & -6+3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(6+3\text{i}){x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0 \\ -15{x}_{1}+(-6+3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(1-3\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}(-2+\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}(-2+\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{\text{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2+\text{i} \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

 

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=1-3\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the  complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=1+3\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2-\text{i} \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}=\frac{(5)(5)}{(-2+\text{i})(-2-\text{i})}=5.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186272076 :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=1+5\text{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ 10 & 6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1+5\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1+5\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5-5\text{i} & -5 \\ 10 & 5-5\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(-5-5\text{i}){x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}=0 \\ 10{x}_{1}+(5-5\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(1+5\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}(1-\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}(1-\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=1+5\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=1-5\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}=\frac{(1-\text{i})(1+\text{i})}{(-2)(-2)}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176975 :tutorial/content "Let's find the eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-\textrm{i}$ of the matrix ![](images/a3/a351d711bda1d0b7009e0c2aa9ac8265e061e103f24dc2ff8c221711189a57e7.svg)

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-\textrm{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} & -1 \\ 2 & -1+\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(1+\text{i}){x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+(-1+\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-\textrm{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another.

As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
x_2 = (1+\textrm{i})x_1.
$$

Therefore, by setting $x_1\in\mathbb C$ to be the free variable, we find that the general solution to our system is given by

![](images/8e/8eef5a23053809341f427e7099c364d65fa24d8144e4feac2a9d817accaa5a88.svg)

Setting $x_1=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

![](images/40/40c4333ba45ec2afa3479f682fcba72c2b61d69c4a4611b30b0d4078731e0a8b.svg)

Notice that our eigenvector has complex-valued entries.

**Note:** To check our result, we can show that $A\mathbf v = \lambda \mathbf v.$ Computing $A\mathbf v,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1-\text{i}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and computing $\lambda \mathbf v$ gives

![](images/12/12fed2087f821e6e5da14d844b61e8300c8a4dc98ac4eff96f719fcc5795b5b4.svg)

So $A\mathbf v = \lambda \mathbf v,$ as required." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176123 :activity/expected-seconds 960.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-\textrm{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} & -1 \\ 2 & -1+\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(1+\text{i}){x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+(-1+\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-\textrm{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another.

As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
x_2 = (1+\textrm{i})x_1.
$$

Therefore, by setting $x_1\in\mathbb C$ to be the free variable, we find that the general solution to our system is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (1+\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}]
$$

Setting $x_1=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that our eigenvector has complex-valued entries.

**Note:** To check our result, we can show that $A\mathbf v = \lambda \mathbf v.$ Computing $A\mathbf v,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1-\text{i}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and computing $\lambda \mathbf v$ gives

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}]
$$

So $A\mathbf v = \lambda \mathbf v,$ as required."]]}

that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-3+4\textrm{i}.$" :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-3+4\textrm{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ -4 & -3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-3+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -3+4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4\text{i} & 4 \\ -4 & -4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-4\text{i}{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}-4\text{i}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-3+4\textrm{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another.

As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
x_1 = -\textrm{i}x_2.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

![](images/0d/0d2e7b9f7011624cf74762419efd784144cf41e2000301d093e1aa612e96f495.png)

:question/problem "If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}10 & 4 \\ -26 & -10\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$" :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-2\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 4 \\ -26 & -10\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10+2\text{i} & 4 \\ -26 & -10+2\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(10+2\text{i}){x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ -26{x}_{1}+(-10+2\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A+2\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}(5+\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -\frac{1}{2}(5+\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{5+\text{i}}{-2}=-\frac{5}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\text{i}.$"} {:db/id 17592186272074 :question/id #uuid "015b39ab-328e-51c1-8903-e3d3a737ea7a" :question/math-academy-id "q-140385"} \begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 \\ 13 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-1+3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -1+3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2-3\text{i} & -1 \\ 13 & 2-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-2-3\text{i}){x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0 \\ 13{x}_{1}+(2-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-1+3\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-2-3\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -(2+3\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2+3\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda_1 =4+5\textrm{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ -5 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4+5\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 4+5\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5\text{i} & 5 \\ -5 & -5\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-5\text{i}{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}-5\text{i}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(4+5\textrm{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another.

As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
x_2 = \textrm{i}x_1.
$$

So, the general solution is given by

![](images/b2/b212192b142e9b4686a4d39e5957db5f3bfbca6283bfcb1d88a6fc57a4a27848.png)

Setting $x_1=1,$ we get the eigenvector

![](images/65/65c073a60a27234349281e873958c2c9d54fb703331a4de23cc358a3eab1b232.png) 

Now, since $\lambda_1=4+5\textrm{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the complex conjugate of $\lambda_1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\lambda_2=\overline{\lambda_1}=4-5\textrm{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector must be the complex conjugate of $\mathbf v_1.$ Therefore, we have

![](images/ca/ca11ae0cca8d07c026108e71b96398171597f7330cb2390d871a8071e7bba873.png)

Finally, we obtain

$$
{\dfrac{a_1a_2}{b_1b_2}} = {\dfrac{(1)(1)}{(\textrm{i})(-\textrm{i})}} = 1.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186176479 :question/id #uuid "597496aa-43f1-55f6-97dc-9702fffad14f" :question/math-academy-id "q-38478"} {:db/id 17592186176480 :question/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Let ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ 10 & 6\end{aligned}].$
Given that ${\lambda }_{1}=1+5\text{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}.$" :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=1+5\text{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ 10 & 6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1+5\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1+5\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5-5\text{i} & -5 \\ 10 & 5-5\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-5-5\text{i}){x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}=0 \\ 10{x}_{1}+(5-5\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(1+5\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}(1-\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}(1-\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=1+5\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=1-5\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}=\frac{(1-\text{i})(1+\text{i})}{(-2)(-2)}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186272077 :question/id #uuid "8845c35f-ffc0-56f1-b7af-e5bdef685e2b" :question/math-academy-id "q-140388" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "011ee86d-97e1-53d3-a3b6-63ede2abaf4d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{4}" :db/id 17592186269268} {:answer/id #uuid "06c071d9-5963-5866-8063-d0604b2c6652" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{25}{16}" :db/id 17592186269329} {:answer/id #uuid "8a5b6a67-1956-5bd6-bf81-18c5c5717aec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{3}" :db/id 17592186270464} {:answer/id #uuid "9b8004b4-6cab-5417-9d66-a6e51002060e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{25}{9}" :db/id 17592186270640} {:answer/id #uuid "c4a5fd11-7f6b-58c9-94e4-6d1dc39b30af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{16}{9}" :db/id 17592186271007}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186269268} :answer-field/id #uuid "21591163-e34d-5795-bc94-436e957ba0e4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186271570}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Given that ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}],$
what is the value of $\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & 4 \\ -5 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-(4)(-5) & =0 \\ 21-7\lambda -3\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +41 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-(-10)\pm \sqrt{(-10)^{2}-4(1)(41)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-(-10)\pm \sqrt{-64}}{2} \\  & =\frac{10\pm 8\text{i}}{2} \\  & =5\pm 4\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =5\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5+4\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 5+4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-4\text{i} & 4 \\ -5 & -2-4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(2-4\text{i}){x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+(-2-4\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(5+4\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}(-2-4\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}(-2-4\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2+4\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=5-4\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2-4\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-5)(-5)}{(2+4\text{i})(2-4\text{i})}=\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186326684 :question/id #uuid "d55b44c8-8d42-5261-b22a-10b38f009304" :question/math-academy-id "q-38494"} {:db/id 17592186326746 :question/id #uuid $$

$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{2\pm \sqrt{(-2)^{2}-4(1)(17)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{2\pm \sqrt{-64}}{2} \\  & =\frac{2\pm 8\text{i}}{2} \\  & =1\pm 4\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =1\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1+4\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1+4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4\text{i} & 8 \\ -2 & -4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}-4\text{i}{x}_{1}+8{x}_{2}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}-4\text{i}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(1+4\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. $$
{x}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}\text{i}{x}_{1}
$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ \frac{1}{2}\text{i}{x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ \text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}} & =\frac{(2)(2)}{(\text{i})(-\text{i})}=4.\end{aligned}

{:db/id 17592186176678 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176975 :tutorial/content "Let's find the eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-\textrm{i}$ of the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-\textrm{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} & -1 \\ 2 & -1+\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(1+\text{i}){x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+(-1+\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-\textrm{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another.

As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
x_2 = (1+\textrm{i})x_1.
$$

Therefore, by setting $x_1\in\mathbb C$ to be the free variable, we find that the general solution to our system is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (1+\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}]
$$

Setting $x_1=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that our eigenvector has complex-valued entries.

**Note:** To check our result, we can show that $A\mathbf v = \lambda \mathbf v.$ Computing $A\mathbf v,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1-\text{i}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and computing $\lambda \mathbf v$ gives

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}]
$$

So $A\mathbf v = \lambda \mathbf v,$ as required." :tutorial/id #uuid "1bde3a85-d8df-5194-8581-77fe2108627c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4297 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "8f4ddd6c-a17e-54f3-bade-a64685e04b36" :step/math-academy-id 26123 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176644}}] :activity/title "Finding Complex Eigenvectors of Real 2x2 Matrices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186176123} {:db/id 17592186176678 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176975 :tutorial/content "Let's find the eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-\textrm{i}$ of the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]$

"3ddd6359-72c0-5eee-87d9-df029bef4a21" :step/math-academy-id 20164 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176643}} {:db/id 17592186176975 :tutorial/content "Let's find the eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-\textrm{i}$ of the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-\textrm{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} & -1 \\ 2 & -1+\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(1+\text{i}){x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+(-1+\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-\textrm{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another.

As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
x_2 = (1+\textrm{i})x_1.
$$

Therefore, by setting $x_1\in\mathbb C$ to be the free variable, we find that the general solution to our system is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (1+\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}]
$$

Setting $x_1=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that our eigenvector has complex-valued entries.

**Note:** To check our result, we can show that $A\mathbf v = \lambda \mathbf v.$ Computing $A\mathbf v,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1-\text{i}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and computing $\lambda \mathbf v$ gives

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}]
$$

So $A\mathbf v = \lambda \mathbf v,$ as required." :tutorial/id #uuid "1bde3a85-d8df-5194-8581-77fe2108627c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4297 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046673} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186411587} :activity/id #uuid "3099b967-b00c-5782-9a83-fd84f9ad579c" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048973 :topic/id #uuid "d050a7cc-fb5e-58e5-a1a7-41ca68d4da28" :topic/math-academy-id 3574} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186411585 :step/content {:db/id 17592186351252 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0489168e-93f4-5458-8a02-7bdcd1fa6253" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186348487} {:answer/id #uuid "4f637c61-750b-5562-b8aa-12c7f8e8f1af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\text{i}" :db/id 17592186349164} {:answer/id #uuid "733e337e-a48f-5c12-902f-9d1678192174" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1+\text{i}" :db/id 17592186349506} {:answer/id #uuid "dc6761e2-57cb-5fcc-9965-269be85a60a1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{i}" :db/id 17592186350374} {:answer/id #uuid "f3b3ce77-31f6-5c5b-9f4d-8e85c892abd9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186350580}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186350374} :answer-field/id #uuid "674d76e0-0dad-52e1-9b92-041ef1633c77" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186350876}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "fbfe9a5f-3d3d-54aa-9e82-2b9e587c84ba" :question/math-academy-id "q-81185" :question/problem "If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of

$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}],$
what is the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 8 \\ -2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-(-2)(8) & =0 \\ 1-2\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +17 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{2\pm \sqrt{(-2)^{2}-4(1)(17)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{2\pm \sqrt{-64}}{2} \\  & =\frac{2\pm 8\text{i}}{2} \\  & =1\pm 4\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =1\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1+4\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1+4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4\text{i} & 8 \\ -2 & -4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-4\text{i}{x}_{1}+8{x}_{2}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}-4\text{i}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(1+4\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}\text{i}{x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ \frac{1}{2}\text{i}{x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=2,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ \text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=1-4\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}} & =\frac{(2)(2)}{(\text{i})(-\text{i})}=4.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "741564cd-c2f1-5aee-8b62-848c21e617d3" :step/next {:db/id 17592186411588}} {:db/id 17592186411587 :step/content {:db/id 17592186411584 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "006f21ef-bd9e-5319-853e-7e3fc38e4a67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lambda =\text{i}" :db/id 17592186411578} {:answer/id #uuid "4cc31227-522c-5e3c-865f-858998fd51d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$v$ is not an eigenvector of $A$" :db/id 17592186411579} {:answer/id #uuid "b38f6e8b-7681-58f7-b559-5a8bae4dff01" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lambda =4" :db/id 17592186411580} {:answer/id #uuid "c4dc0bd2-9334-5cf0-9566-65f6c6862a8a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lambda =-2\text{i}" :db/id 17592186411581} {:answer/id #uuid "fa45e365-566e-56f7-88cc-77bf8156b5ec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lambda =4\text{i}" :db/id 17592186411582}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186411582} :answer-field/id #uuid "93c408a0-c9c5-54b6-81eb-ee9b40cb4448" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186411583}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "db7154e6-6fda-5907-98f7-b3398371be54" :question/math-academy-id "q-38493" :question/problem "Determine if $v=[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ 4 & -2\end{aligned}].$
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?" :question/worked-solution "The eigenvectors are non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ 4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-8+4\text{i} \\ 8\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8{\text{i}}^{2}+4\text{i} \\ 8\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =4\text{i}[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =4\text{i}v.\end{aligned}

Since $Av=4\text{i}v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =4\text{i}.$"} :step/id #uuid "7c22f243-0739-5a0f-8281-eeed84387bab" :step/next {:db/id 17592186411589}} {:db/id 17592186411588 :step/content {:db/id 17592186272077 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "011ee86d-97e1-53d3-a3b6-63ede2abaf4d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{4}" :db/id 17592186269268} {:answer/id #uuid "06c071d9-5963-5866-8063-d0604b2c6652" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{25}{16}" :db/id 17592186269329} {:answer/id #uuid "8a5b6a67-1956-5bd6-bf81-18c5c5717aec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{3}" :db/id 17592186270464} {:answer/id #uuid "9b8004b4-6cab-5417-9d66-a6e51002060e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{25}{9}" :db/id 17592186270640} {:answer/id #uuid "c4a5fd11-7f6b-58c9-94e4-6d1dc39b30af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{16}{9}" :db/id 17592186271007}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186269268} :answer-field/id #uuid "21591163-e34d-5795-bc94-436e957ba0e4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186271570}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "8845c35f-ffc0-56f1-b7af-e5bdef685e2b" :question/math-academy-id "q-140388" :question/problem "Given that ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}],$
what is the value of $\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & 4 \\ -5 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-(4)(-5) & =0 \\ 21-7\lambda -3\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +41 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-(-10)\pm \sqrt{(-10)^{2}-4(1)(41)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-(-10)\pm \sqrt{-64}}{2} \\  & =\frac{10\pm 8\text{i}}{2} \\  & =5\pm 4\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =5\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5+4\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 5+4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2-4\text{i} & 4 \\ -5 & -2-4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(2-4\text{i}){x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+(-2-4\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(5+4\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}(-2-4\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}(-2-4\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2+4\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=5-4\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2-4\text{i} \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}} & =\frac{(-5)(-5)}{(2+4\text{i})(2-4\text{i})}=\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d4502c0c-e4ff-5fb4-9162-5b78360320c6"} {:db/id 17592186411589 :step/content {:db/id 17592186326744 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5e967569-f453-574e-8919-a67fad95d2f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lambda =13\text{i}" :db/id 17592186324758} {:answer/id #uuid "7b6f6a10-0bd5-5a15-8100-84cdb1b48c99" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lambda =7\text{i}" :db/id 17592186325009} {:answer/id #uuid "8a1224cc-38c3-56bc-8a03-7ccf158de176" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$v$ is not an eigenvector of $A$" :db/id 17592186325145} {:answer/id #uuid "ca079c89-eb27-58a1-8df2-a13f57b8062e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lambda =-7\text{i}" :db/id 17592186325722} {:answer/id #uuid "e251a6af-588a-5940-924b-907ba00680c6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\lambda =-13\text{i}" :db/id 17592186325954}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186325009} :answer-field/id #uuid "d985c21d-6faa-5e92-8ab4-fa9bd7e30639" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326615}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "0ea0f7da-291a-5ef5-afec-bc983b4386ad" :question/math-academy-id "q-39181" :question/problem "Determine whether $v=[\begin{aligned}-4+7\text{i} \\ 13\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ 13 & 4\end{aligned}].$

matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ 13 & 4\end{aligned}].$
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?" :question/worked-solution "The eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ 13 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4+7\text{i} \\ 13\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-49-28\text{i} \\ 91\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}49{\text{i}}^{2}-28\text{i} \\ 91\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =7\text{i}[\begin{aligned}-4+7\text{i} \\ 13\end{aligned}] \\  & =7\text{i}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=7\text{i}v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =7\text{i}.$"} :step/id #uuid "db758ac7-852d-51b4-ad30-e5acef4cfcd0" :step/next 17592186046954 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1005 17592186046982 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1007 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I" 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I develops the core mathematical structures and analytical tools used throughout theoretical and applied physics. Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.
Students learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.
Students then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.
The course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.
The course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.
Students then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.
The final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating strings, mechanical systems, and electromagnetic circuits." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1012 154 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1013 "PS1" 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1014 #uuid [17592186046673 1005 17592186046961 17592186045417] [17592186046673 1005 17592186046979 17592186045417] [17592186046673 1007 "Methods of Proof" 17592186045417] [17592186046673 1008 "This course introduces students to proof-writing essentials, bridging the gap between pure problem-solving and constructing formal mathematical arguments. Students will formalize their understanding of logic, sets, and functions while delving into new concepts such as congruence, relations, and cardinality.
This course serves as ideal preparation for students wishing to pursue undergraduate studies in formal mathematical disciplines, including Discrete Mathematics, Abstract Algebra, and Real Analysis.
The prerequisite for Methods of Proof is single-variable calculus, which would be satisfied by completion of either Calculus II, AP Calculus BC, or Mathematical Foundations III." 17592186045417] [17592186046673 1009 "Students begin by mastering the basics of logic and logical operations, including statements, predicates, connectives, logical laws, logical equivalence, conditional and biconditional statements, quantifiers, inference, and formal and informal language. By solidifying their grasp of these logical fundamentals, students will have a secure underpinning that enables them to embark on their journey into proof-writing confidently.
A robust knowledge of set theory is another cornerstone of mathematical proof-writing. Students will extend and formalize their understanding of sets and learn to translate between logical and set operations. By the end of the course, students will appreciate how set theory provides a comprehensive toolkit for proving mathematical results.
After mastering these fundamentals, students will explore various proof-writing techniques, including direct proof, proof by cases, proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction, disproof, and mathematical induction. The course emphasizes proving concepts related to parity, divisibility, congruence, sequences, functions, set identities, and relations. Students will have multiple opportunities to test and refine their proof construction and comprehension skills throughout the course and in varied contexts
This challenging yet engaging course helps students with strong mathematical foundations build a solid base for further progression into advanced undergraduate courses." 17592186045417]
